questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explain: Canberra, in the Australian Capital Territory, is Australia's capital city. It is home to several national institutions, including Parliament House and the High Court of Australia, and lies between Sydney and Melbourne.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many states and mainland territories make up Australia?
options: Six states and two mainland territories
questions.explain: The Commonwealth of Australia is a federation made up of six states and two mainland territories. Canberra is the national capital, and each state and mainland territory also has its own capital city.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: When is Australia Day celebrated?
questions.explain: Australia Day is celebrated on 26 January each year and is a public holiday in every state and territory. It marks the anniversary of the arrival of the First Fleet from Great Britain in 1788.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: On which date is Anzac Day commemorated?
questions.explain: Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April, the date in 1915 when Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye during World War I. It is a solemn day to remember all who served and died in wars.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national flower?
questions.explain: The golden wattle is Australia's national flower. This small tree grows mainly in south-eastern Australia and has bright green leaves and many golden yellow flowers in spring. Each state and territory also has its own floral emblem.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who were the first inhabitants of Australia?
options: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explain: Australia's first inhabitants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, whose cultures and traditions are the oldest continuous cultures in the world. They have a deep connection with the land, expressed in stories, art and dance.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Where do Torres Strait Islander people come from?
options: Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea
The western coast of Western Australia
questions.explain: Torres Strait Islander people come from the islands lying between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea. Aboriginal people, historically, are from mainland Australia and Tasmania. Together they are Australia's first peoples.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: According to the archaeological record, when did Aboriginal peoples arrive in Australia?
questions.explain: The archaeological record indicates that Aboriginal peoples arrived in Australia between 65,000 and 40,000 years ago. Aboriginal peoples themselves believe they are central to the creation stories of this land, which begin with the beginning of time.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many convict ships made up the First Fleet that arrived from Great Britain in 1788?
questions.explain: European settlement began when the First Fleet of 11 convict ships arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788. British jails were overcrowded, so the government transported convicts to the new colony of New South Wales.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales?
questions.explain: Captain Arthur Phillip was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales. The colony survived and grew as more convicts and free settlers arrived, and further colonies were later set up in other parts of Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: In which year did a gold rush begin in the colonies of New South Wales and Victoria?
questions.explain: A gold rush began in 1851 when gold was discovered in New South Wales and Victoria. People came from all around the world to seek their fortune, and within ten years Australia's population had more than doubled.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: During the gold rush, which group became the first large group of migrants not from Europe?
questions.explain: Chinese people who arrived in the colonies during the gold rush of the 1850s were the first large group of migrants to Australia who did not come from Europe. They added to the growing diversity of the colonies.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: After which event were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples included in official estimates of Australia's population?
options: The end of World War II
questions.explain: In 1901 Australia's population of about four million did not include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. It was only after a Referendum in 1967 that they were included in official estimates of the Australian population.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What brought a wave of non-British migration to Australia after World War II?
options: The opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge
Millions of people in Europe had to leave their homelands
questions.explain: After World War II, millions of people in Europe were forced to leave their homelands. Large numbers of Europeans came to Australia to build a new life, creating a wave of non-British migration.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national language?
questions.explain: English is Australia's national language and part of its national identity. Communicating in English is important for making the most of living and working in Australia, and in keeping with Australian values migrants should learn and use English.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages does the guide say are valued in Australia?
questions.explain: While English is the national language, other languages are also valued in Australia. These include more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, part of the oldest continuous cultures in the world.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which was the first colony established by the British in Australia?
questions.explain: New South Wales was the first colony established by the British. Its capital, Sydney, is the nation's largest city, and the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Opera House are national icons.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which is the smallest of the mainland states?
questions.explain: Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states and its capital is Melbourne. Many fine buildings in Victoria were built from the wealth of the 1850s gold rush, and its icons include the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the 12 Apostles.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which is the largest state in Australia?
questions.explain: Western Australia is the largest state and its capital is Perth. The east of the state is mostly desert, while the south-west is a rich farming and wine-growing area. It is home to many large mining projects.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: The Great Barrier Reef runs along the coast of which state?
questions.explain: The world-famous Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland's eastern coast. Queensland is the second largest state, its capital is Brisbane, and it has tropical rainforests, temperate coastal areas and an often dry inland.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland?
questions.explain: Tasmania, the smallest state, is an island separated from the mainland by the Bass Strait. Its capital is Hobart, much of the island is unspoilt wilderness, and its icons include Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur and the Bay of Fires.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of which part of Australia?
questions.explain: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of the Northern Territory. The territory has a tropical environment in the north and dry red desert in the south, and its capital city is Darwin.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who performs a Welcome to Country?
options: An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region
questions.explain: A Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local area, welcoming visitors to their traditional land. It can include songs, dances, smoking ceremonies or speeches and usually opens an event.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: During Australia Day celebrations, who announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra?
questions.explain: During Australia Day celebrations, the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra. Australia Day is also marked by events across the country, including special citizenship ceremonies.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Anzac Day takes its name from which military force?
options: The Australian Navy and Air Corps
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
questions.explain: Anzac Day is named after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, which landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye during World War I. On this day Australians remember the sacrifice of all who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What do the seven points of the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: The seven days of the week
The six states and the territories
questions.explain: The Commonwealth Star, beneath the Union Jack on the Australian National Flag, has seven points. Six points represent the six states and one point represents the territories. The Southern Cross appears on the right of the flag.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the yellow circle represent?
questions.explain: The Australian Aboriginal Flag is black, red and yellow. The black top half represents the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, the red bottom half represents the earth, which has ceremonial significance, and the yellow circle represents the sun.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which two native animals support the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explain: On the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, a kangaroo and an emu, both native animals, support the shield, which represents the six states and federation. A gold Commonwealth Star sits above, against a background of golden wattle.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national gemstone?
questions.explain: The opal is Australia's national gemstone. According to Aboriginal legend, a rainbow touched the earth and created the colours of the opal, a stone known for its shifting flashes of colour.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is the title of Australia's national anthem?
questions.explain: 'Advance Australia Fair' is Australia's national anthem. It is sung on occasions of national importance, including at Australian citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events. Everyone sings it at a citizenship ceremony.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: For Australian citizens aged 18 or over, enrolling and voting in federal elections is…
questions.explain: Australian citizens aged 18 or over must enrol and vote in federal and state or territory elections and in referendums. Voting gives citizens a say in how Australia is governed. Voting in some local government elections may not be compulsory.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What is Australia's system of government?
questions.explain: Australia's system of government is a parliamentary democracy. The power of the government comes from the Australian people, because Australian citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament. Elected representatives make the laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, how do representatives answer to the people for their decisions?
options: They do not answer to anyone
questions.explain: Representatives in parliament must answer to the people, through elections, for the decisions they make. If voters are unhappy with their representatives, they can choose someone else at the next election.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How do Australians believe change in society or the law should come about?
options: Through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process
questions.explain: Australians are proud to live in a peaceful country with a stable system of government. They believe change should occur through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process, and they reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How are all Australians expected to treat each other, whatever their race, gender, age, religion or background?
options: According to their country of origin
With suspicion until trust is earned
questions.explain: Australia's democratic system is based on every individual having rights and equality under the law. All Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect, regardless of race, origin, gender, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion or wealth.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Respect for all individuals regardless of background

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Under freedom of speech, can people in Australia criticise the government?
options: No, it is against the law
Yes, as long as they obey Australian laws
questions.explain: Freedom of speech means people can say and write what they think. For example, they can criticise the government, protest peacefully against its decisions and campaign to change laws, as long as they still obey Australian laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Freedom of expression in Australia includes expressing views through which means?
questions.explain: Freedom of expression means people can express their views, including through art, film, music and literature. People are also free to meet in public or private places for social or political discussion, while always obeying the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: When people gather to protest against a government action, what must the gathering be like?
options: Peaceful, without injuring anyone or damaging property
Limited to members of one political party
questions.explain: Australians can gather with others to protest against a government action or an organisation. The laws of Australia must always be obeyed, which means such gatherings must be peaceful and must not injure any person or damage property.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How does the guide describe Australia's religious heritage?
questions.explain: Australia has a Judaeo-Christian heritage and many Australians describe themselves as Christians, but there are people in Australia from all the large religions. The government and the law treat all citizens equally, whatever their beliefs.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these is a public holiday in Australia on a Christian day?
questions.explain: Reflecting its Judaeo-Christian heritage, Australia has public holidays on Christian days such as Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day. People of all faiths, and of none, are free to practise their own beliefs.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: The government in Australia is secular. What does this mean?
options: It operates separately from churches and other religious entities
It is run by church leaders
questions.explain: Australia's government is secular, which means it operates separately from churches and other religious bodies. There is no official national religion, and the government treats all citizens equally whatever their religion or beliefs.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? People in Australia are required to follow a religion.
questions.explain: The statement is false. People in Australia are free to follow any religion they choose, and they may also choose not to follow a religion at all. In every case, religious or not, the laws of Australia must be obeyed.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What does a 'fair go' mean in Australia?
options: What people achieve should come from their talents, work and effort, not their wealth or background
Only citizens may own a business
questions.explain: Australians value equal opportunity, often called a 'fair go'. What someone achieves in life should result from their talents, work and effort rather than their wealth or background, so that there are no formal class distinctions in Australian society.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Australian law protects people from being treated differently because of which characteristics?
questions.explain: There are a number of laws in Australia that ensure a person is not treated differently to others because of their gender, race, disability or age. Equal treatment under the law is one of Australia's core democratic principles.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary. What is the related responsibility of Australian citizens?
options: To serve in the army for two years
To pay a defence fee instead
To defend Australia should the need arise
questions.explain: Although service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary, Australian citizens have a responsibility to defend Australia should the need arise. It is vital that citizens are committed to joining together to defend the nation and its way of life.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Defend Australia should the need arise

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which Australian citizens can be called to serve on a jury?
options: Citizens who are on the electoral roll
questions.explain: Jury service, if requested, is a responsibility for Australian citizens aged 18 or over. Citizens on the electoral roll can be called to serve. A jury of ordinary men and women hears the evidence and decides whether a person is guilty or not guilty.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Serve on a jury if called to do so

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What is a referendum?
options: A vote to choose a new Prime Minister
A vote to change the Australian Constitution
A survey run by a newspaper
questions.explain: A referendum is a vote to change the Australian Constitution. Voting in a referendum is a responsibility of Australian citizens aged 18 or over, just like voting in federal and state or territory elections.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is voting compulsory in every Australian election?
options: It is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections, but may not be in some local government elections
Only for people born in Australia
questions.explain: Voting is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections. However, it may not be compulsory to vote in local government elections in some states. Voting gives citizens a say in how Australia is governed.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which is a privilege of Australian citizenship relating to children born overseas?
options: Their automatic exemption from all taxes
Their right to vote from age 12
Applying for them to become Australian citizens by descent
questions.explain: Australian citizens can apply for their child born overseas to become an Australian citizen by descent. It is one of the privileges of citizenship, alongside voting, seeking election and holding an Australian passport.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for children born overseas to become Australian citizens by descent

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which is an example of working in the Australian Public Service, a privilege of citizenship?
options: Working for the Australian Taxation Office
questions.explain: A privilege of Australian citizenship is to apply for a job in the Australian Public Service and work for the Australian Government, for example in Services Australia or the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which three services make up the Australian Defence Force?
options: The Army, Navy and Air Force
The Navy, Customs and Border Force
The Air Force, Fire Brigade and Ambulance
questions.explain: Australian citizens have the right to apply for a job in the Australian Defence Force, which is made up of the Army, the Navy and the Air Force. Service in the Defence Force is voluntary.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which Australian citizens CANNOT seek election to parliament?
questions.explain: Australian citizens aged 18 or over who are not dual citizens can seek election to parliament at federal, state or territory level. Serving in an Australian parliament is described as both an honour and a serious responsibility.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: If you travel overseas as an Australian citizen, what do you need to return to Australia?
options: No visa: you are free to return
questions.explain: Australian citizens have the right to live freely in Australia and the privilege to apply for an Australian passport. If they travel overseas, they are free to return to Australia without needing a visa.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for an Australian passport and re-enter Australia freely

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: While overseas, where can an Australian citizen ask for help from an Australian government official in times of need?
options: An Australian embassy, high commission or consulate
questions.explain: In many countries Australia has an embassy, high commission or consulate. Australian officials can help citizens in emergencies such as civil unrest or natural disasters, issue emergency passports and give support after an accident, serious illness or death.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: When an Australian citizen is in another country, whose laws must they obey?
questions.explain: Australian citizens can seek consular help from Australian officials while overseas, but when in another country they must obey the laws of that country. Consular assistance does not place a person above local law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which agency collects tax paid on money earned from a job, a business or investments?
questions.explain: Paying tax is required by law and is an important way to contribute to the Australian community. Tax is paid on money earned from a job, a business or investments and is collected by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these services are paid for through taxes in Australia?
options: Government-funded healthcare and education, defence, roads and social security
questions.explain: Many benefits that Australians enjoy are made possible through taxes. Taxes pay for government-funded healthcare and education, defence, roads and railways, and social security. State and territory governments and local councils also collect taxes for services.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these is an example of actively participating in Australian society?
options: Volunteering to do social and community work
questions.explain: Australia encourages all citizens to participate actively in society. Examples include joining neighbourhood and community organisations, volunteering for social and community work, joining an arts or cultural group and taking part in political life.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is tax in Australia paid only on wages from a job?
options: No, there are also taxes on many goods and services
questions.explain: Tax is paid on money earned from a job, a business or investments, and there are also taxes on many goods and services. The ATO works to make sure people know their tax rights and obligations and pay the correct amount.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Why do our representatives in government make laws?
options: To benefit only the governing party
To maintain an orderly, free and safe society and protect our rights
To limit who can live in each state
questions.explain: Representatives in government make laws to maintain an orderly, free and safe society and to protect people's rights. All Australian citizens, and other people in Australia, must obey the laws of Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Obey the laws of Australia

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: On what date did the colonies unite as the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.explain: On 1 January 1901 the Australian Constitution came into effect and the six colonies became one independent nation, the Commonwealth of Australia. The national parliament, government and High Court were established at this time.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: How many senators does each state elect?
questions.explain: All states are equally represented in the Senate, whatever their size or population. Each state elects 12 senators and the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory elect two each, giving 76 senators in total.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who signs a Bill so that it becomes law (Royal Assent)?
questions.explain: A proposed law, called a Bill, must be agreed by a majority in both Houses of Parliament. It then goes to the Governor-General, whose signature, known as Royal Assent, turns the Bill into law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which level of government is mainly responsible for hospitals and schools?
questions.explain: State and territory governments are primarily responsible for hospitals and health services, schools, roads and railways, forestry, police and ambulance services, and public transport. Other services belong to the Australian Government or local councils.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which agency conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll?
options: The Department of the Prime Minister
questions.explain: The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) is a Commonwealth agency that runs federal elections and referendums and keeps the electoral roll. It is independent, so political parties and people in government cannot influence its decisions.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How do I have my say?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In Australia, voting in an election is by secret ballot. What does this mean?
options: No one is allowed to know whom you voted for unless you choose to tell them
Votes are counted in secret by the government
Only some people are told about the election
Candidates are kept secret until election day
questions.explain: Voting in Australia is by secret ballot, so voters are free and safe to vote for any candidate. No one is allowed to know whom you have voted for, unless you decide to tell them yourself.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How do I have my say?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Before 1901, how was Australia made up?
options: Two large colonies, east and west
questions.explain: After British settlement and before 1901, Australia was made up of six separate, self-governing British colonies, each with its own constitution and laws on defence, immigration, postage, trade and transport. This created difficulties between them.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which court did the Australian Constitution establish, with the ultimate power to apply and interpret the laws of Australia?
options: The Supreme Court of New South Wales
questions.explain: The Australian Constitution set up the Parliament of the Commonwealth, made up of a House of Representatives and a Senate. It also established the High Court of Australia, which has the ultimate power to apply and interpret Australia's laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is needed in a referendum for the Australian Constitution to be changed?
options: The agreement of the Prime Minister alone
A two-thirds vote in the Senate only
A majority of voters in New South Wales
A 'double majority': a majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in a majority of states
questions.explain: In a referendum, a 'double majority' is required. A majority of voters across the nation must vote for the change, and a majority of voters in a majority of the states must also vote for it.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Why does the Australian Constitution divide the power of government into legislative, executive and judicial powers?
options: To stop one person or group from holding all the power
To give the King more control
To allow the states to ignore federal law
questions.explain: The Constitution divides government power between the legislative (Parliament), the executive (such as the Prime Minister and Cabinet) and the judicial (judges). This separation prevents any one person or group from holding all the power.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the power of government controlled?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: On whose advice does the King of Australia appoint the Governor-General?
options: The Premier of New South Wales
questions.explain: The King of Australia appoints the Governor-General as his representative in Australia, acting on the advice of the Australian Prime Minister. The Governor-General acts independently of all political parties and must remain neutral.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who represents the King in each Australian state?
questions.explain: In each of the six states there is a Governor who represents the King, in a role similar to that of the Governor-General at the national level. The King does not have a day-to-day role in government.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which of these is part of the Governor-General's role?
options: Acting as Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force
questions.explain: The Governor-General is not part of the government and must remain neutral. The role includes signing Bills into law, ceremonial duties, approving the appointment of ministers and federal judges, starting the process for a federal election and acting as Commander-in-Chief of the ADF.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: The role of the Governor-General

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is the title of the leader of a state government?
questions.explain: The leader of a state government is called the Premier. The leader of a territory government is the Chief Minister, and the leader of a local government is a Mayor or Shire President.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which is another name for the Senate?
questions.explain: The Senate is sometimes called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House. The House of Representatives, by contrast, is also known as the Lower House or the People's House.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is a key difference between Australian states and self-governing territories?
options: Territory laws can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government at any time
Territories are ruled by the King directly
questions.explain: States have rights recognised by the Constitution, while territories do not. States can pass laws in their own right, but laws made by self-governing territories can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government at any time.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which level of government is responsible for immigration and citizenship?
questions.explain: The Australian Government is responsible for matters including taxation, immigration and citizenship, defence, foreign affairs, social security, postal services, trade, and airports and air safety. States and local councils deal with other services.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: After a federal election, who generally forms the Australian Government?
options: The party or coalition with the majority of members in the House of Representatives
The party with the most senators
The party chosen by the Governor-General personally
The party with the oldest leader
questions.explain: After a federal election, the government is generally formed by the party or coalition of parties with the majority of members in the House of Representatives. The leader of that party becomes Prime Minister.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who forms the Opposition after a federal election?
options: The party or coalition with the second largest number of members in the House of Representatives
Members chosen by the High Court
questions.explain: The party or coalition with the second largest number of members in the House of Representatives forms the Opposition. Its leader is called the Leader of the Opposition, and it scrutinises the work of the government.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: When a member of parliament proposes a new law or a change to an existing one, what is the proposal called?
questions.explain: A proposal to introduce a new law or change an existing one is called a Bill. Both Houses of Parliament consider, debate and vote on it, and if a majority in each agrees, it goes to the Governor-General for Royal Assent.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Judges and magistrates are appointed by the government. Can the government remove them because it disagrees with their decisions?
options: Only if the Prime Minister agrees
questions.explain: Judges and magistrates are the highest authority in a court. They are independent and no one can tell them what to decide. Although the government appoints them, it cannot take their jobs away if it disagrees with their decisions.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In Australia's court system, how is a person treated until they are found guilty in a court?
questions.explain: In Australia's court system, people are considered innocent until they are found guilty in a court. Every person also has the right to be represented by a lawyer in court.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In a criminal trial, if the jury finds a person guilty, who decides the penalty?
questions.explain: A jury is a group of ordinary citizens randomly chosen from the population. The judge explains the law to the jury, the jury decides whether a person is innocent or guilty, and in a criminal trial the judge then decides the penalty.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Besides investigating crimes against federal laws, the Australian Federal Police is responsible for general police work in which place?
questions.explain: The Australian Federal Police (AFP) investigates crimes against federal laws, such as drug trafficking and crimes against national security or the environment. It also carries out general police work in the Australian Capital Territory.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In Australia, is it a crime simply to offer a bribe to a police officer?
options: No, only accepting a bribe is a crime
Only if the amount is large
Yes, even offering a bribe is a crime
questions.explain: In Australia it is a serious crime to bribe the police, and it is a crime even to offer a bribe to a police officer. The police are independent of government and have a good relationship with the community.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: If you break an Australian law that you did not know about, can you still be charged?
options: Yes, not knowing the law is no excuse
Only if you are a citizen
questions.explain: It is important to be familiar with the laws of Australia. If you break a law you did not know about, you could still be charged, because not knowing the law is no excuse.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which of these can be a form of domestic and family violence?
options: Isolating a family member from friends and family
questions.explain: Domestic and family violence includes behaviour or threats that aim to control a partner by causing fear or threatening their safety. It can include hitting, isolating a family member from friends and family, or threatening children or pets, and it is against the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who must wear a seatbelt when travelling in a car in Australia?
questions.explain: Everybody travelling in a car in Australia must wear a seatbelt, and babies and young children must be in an approved car seat. Road rules are set by state and territory governments and breaking them can lead to fines or prison.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Is it legal to use a hand-held mobile device while driving in Australia?
options: No, it is against the law
questions.explain: Traffic laws in Australia are very strict. It is against the law to use a hand-held mobile device while driving, and it is also illegal to drive after taking drugs or when above the blood alcohol limit.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What do you need in order to drive a car in Australia?
options: A local driver's licence and a registered car
Only a foreign licence held for ten years
questions.explain: To drive a car in Australia, you must have a local driver's licence and the car must be registered. Road and traffic rules are controlled by state and territory governments, and people can be fined or sent to prison for breaking them.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a religious law override Australian law?
options: No, religious laws have no legal status in Australia
questions.explain: Australia has no official national religion and people may follow any religion they choose. However, religious laws have no legal status in Australia, and Australian law must be followed by everyone, including where it differs from religious law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Do men and women have equal rights in Australia?
questions.explain: Men and women have equal rights in Australia. Both have equal access to education and employment, can vote and stand for parliament, can join the Australian Defence Force and the police, and are treated equally in courts.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is it acceptable to promote violence against a group because of its religion?
questions.explain: It is never acceptable to promote violence against another person or group, for example because of their culture, ethnicity, religion or background. Doing so is against Australian values and against the law, whatever the setting.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under the Rule of Law, who must obey Australian laws?
questions.explain: Under the Rule of Law, all Australians are equal in relation to the law and no person or group is above it. Australian laws apply to all people in Australia, regardless of their background or culture.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a person be forced to join or stay in an organisation?
options: No, joining or leaving is voluntary
questions.explain: In Australia people are free to join or leave any lawful group voluntarily, such as a political party, trade union, or religious, cultural or social group. Individuals cannot be compelled to join an organisation or forced to leave it.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under the Rule of Law, should you obey the law even when no one is watching?
options: No, only when police are present
Only if you agree with the law
questions.explain: Australians recognise the importance of laws for a peaceful and orderly society. Everybody should obey the law and not break it at any time, otherwise they face penalties, and people should follow the law even if no one is watching.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Do newspapers, television and radio in Australia have freedom of speech?
options: No, the government decides what they publish
Yes, they have the same freedom as people, within the law
questions.explain: People in Australia are free to say and write what they think about any topic, within the law. Newspapers, television and radio outlets have the same freedom, which is an important part of Australia's democracy.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is illegal in Australia, even though freedom of speech is valued?
options: Writing a letter to a newspaper
Making false allegations or encouraging others to break the law
questions.explain: Freedom of speech in Australia has limits set by law. It is illegal to make false allegations or to encourage others to break the law, and other people's lawful freedom of speech and expression must always be respected.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is polygamy (being married to more than one person at the same time) legal in Australia?
options: No, it is against the law
Yes, if a religion allows it
Yes, if the marriages took place overseas and are kept private
questions.explain: Some religious or cultural practices are against the law in Australia. Polygamy, which means being married to more than one person at the same time, is illegal and can result in severe legal penalties, including imprisonment.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A family wants to arrange their daughter's marriage without her free consent. What does Australian law say?
options: It is allowed if the family's culture accepts it
Forced marriage is against the law and can lead to imprisonment
It is allowed if a religious leader agrees
It is a private family matter
questions.explain: Forced marriage, in which one or both people do not have a free choice, is against the law in Australia. Like polygamy, it can result in severe legal penalties, including imprisonment, whatever the family's cultural or religious views.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is religious intolerance acceptable in Australian society?
questions.explain: Religious intolerance is not acceptable in Australian society. All people should be given equal opportunity to pursue their goals and interests, regardless of their ethnicity or religion, as long as they are obeying Australian law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: How does Australian law treat people of different faiths, such as Buddhists and Christians?
options: Only the largest religion is protected
questions.explain: The law is applied in Australia so that people from different backgrounds are neither given preferential treatment nor discriminated against. For example, Buddhists and people of all other faiths receive the same treatment as Christians.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under Australian law, can two women marry each other?
options: Only if they were married overseas
questions.explain: Australian society values the equal rights of all people, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Under Australian law, two people can marry each other, including marriage between two men or two women.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A woman and a man apply for the same job. The woman has better qualifications and skills. Is it her right to get the job ahead of the man?
options: No, men must be chosen first
questions.explain: It is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender. In Australia, it is a right for a woman to get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Who has the right to make independent choices about personal matters such as marriage and religion?
options: Only the head of the family
questions.explain: Both men and women in Australia have the right to make their own independent choices about personal matters, such as marriage and religion. They are protected by law from intimidation or violence relating to those choices.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a wife apply to the courts for a divorce even if her husband wishes to continue the marriage?
options: Only with a religious leader's permission
questions.explain: Divorce is acceptable in Australia. Either a husband or a wife may apply to the courts for a divorce, even if the other spouse wishes to continue the marriage. Both spouses have equal rights.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: When an organisation needs to fill a job, whom does the law support it in selecting?
options: The person with the best skills and experience for the job
A member of the owner's family
The applicant with the most money
Someone of the same ethnicity as the manager
questions.explain: What someone achieves should result from hard work and talent. A person should get a job based on skills and experience, not gender, wealth or ethnicity, and the law supports organisations in selecting the person best suited to the job.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A neighbour has opinions and lifestyle choices very different from your own. What do Australian values expect of you?
options: To listen and respect their views, being tolerant where you disagree
To try to make them change
To complain about them to the police
questions.explain: Australia values mutual respect and tolerance. This means respecting the freedom, dignity, opinions and choices of others, listening to them and respecting their views even when they differ from your own.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is verbal abuse of another person acceptable in Australia?
options: Yes, if no one is physically hurt
No, violence of any kind, including verbal abuse, is illegal
Only if the person deserves it
questions.explain: It is against the law to be violent towards another person. Violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, is illegal. Australians believe in peaceful disagreement and the right to be safe from violence and intimidation.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What is the age of sexual consent in Australia?
options: 16 or 17, depending on the state or territory
questions.explain: Australia has very strict laws about the age of sexual consent, which is 16 or 17 depending on the state or territory. For example, a 20 year old man cannot have sexual relations with a 15 year old girl anywhere in Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A police officer makes a lawful request of you. What should you do?
options: Ignore it if you are busy
Obey only if the officer is senior
Ask a friend to respond for you
questions.explain: In Australia, the lawful actions of the police should be supported. You should obey a lawful request from the police, because all Australians commit to following the law. Police protect life and property.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is an example of racism that has no place in Australia?
options: Making racially abusive comments at a sporting event
questions.explain: Racism has no place in Australia. This includes creating or sharing racially offensive material on the internet or in other publications and making racially abusive comments in a public place or at a sporting event.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What responsibility does everyone in Australia have, when they are able to?
options: To rely entirely on government payments
To try to support themselves and their families
To work only for the government
To leave their family's support to others
questions.explain: Australians expect everyone living in Australia to participate in society and make a contribution to the community. Everyone has a responsibility to try to support themselves and their families when they are able to do so.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What does the Australian value of 'mateship' mean?
options: Choosing friends from the same background only
Helping each other, especially in times of need
questions.explain: Australians value 'mateship', which means helping each other in times of need. Examples include taking a meal to an elderly neighbour, driving a friend to a medical appointment or visiting someone who is sick, frail or lonely.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Compassion for those in need

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What must applicants for Australian citizenship whose native language is not English undertake to do?
options: Make reasonable efforts to learn English
questions.explain: English is valued as Australia's national language and a unifying element of society. Applicants for Australian citizenship must undertake to make reasonable efforts to learn English if it is not their native language.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: English as the national language

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: You suspect that a neighbour may be planning to commit a serious crime. What should you do?
options: Report it to Australian government authorities as soon as possible
Ignore it as none of your business
questions.explain: Everyone in Australia has responsibilities to help protect society. If people suspect a friend or neighbour may be planning a serious crime, they should report this to Australian government authorities as soon as possible.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: If a person in Australia sees or knows about a child being abused, what should they do?
options: Report it to the police to investigate
questions.explain: Helping keep society safe includes protecting children. If a person in Australia sees or has knowledge of a child being abused, they should report it to the police so that it can be investigated.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is an example of cyber abuse, many forms of which are illegal in Australia?
options: Posting a holiday photo of yourself
Sending a birthday message to a friend
Sharing sexual photos of someone online without their consent
questions.explain: Online abuse, sometimes called cyber abuse, is not accepted in Australia. Examples include sharing sexual photos or videos online without consent, stalking a person online and making racially abusive comments about someone online.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: An Australian citizen is also a citizen of another country. While in Australia, which laws must they follow?
options: Only the laws of their other country
All Australian laws at all times
questions.explain: Australian citizens may hold dual or multiple citizenship if the laws of the other countries allow it. However, an Australian citizen in Australia must follow all Australian laws at all times, even if they are also a citizen elsewhere.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these would undermine Australia's interests and security?
options: Using social media to share official government secrets
Volunteering at a bushfire relief centre
questions.explain: Australian society is based on shared obligations not to undermine Australia's interests and security. For example, using social media to share official government secrets would undermine Australia's interests and could put others at risk.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
